title: After My Clinical Clerkship at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia
paragraphs: It was the end of March when I landed in Philadelphia, shivering with cold inside my coat but with my heart full of hope for life in the United States and my clinical clerkship. I was given the opportunity to study clinically for three months at the University of Pennsylvania (Penn), one of the Ivy League schools and the oldest comprehensive university in the United States. Mixed in with the local medical students, I did the "elective" course, in which one submits the department one wants to the academic affairs office in advance and trains in that single department for four weeks. Penn has many affiliated hospitals, not only the university hospital, the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania (HUP), but also the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP), counted among the three major children's hospitals on the East Coast, and the Veterans Affairs Medical Center (VAMC), where veterans can receive medical care free of charge, and medical education is carried out in various departments of these hospitals. I was allowed to train at CHOP for all three months. CHOP is known as the first specialised children's hospital in the United States, and last year, 2005, it celebrated its 150th anniversary, with banners celebrating this displayed inside and outside the hospital. It is not merely old: it shines as the No. 1 children's hospital in the country in numerous journals, and it is also popular as a training hospital, where one has to win out in considerable competition to become a fellow or resident. It has its own research centre attached to the hospital, and both basic and clinical research are active. Every day at noon, conferences centred on lectures and case reports for residents and students were held, and every Wednesday morning a lecture for all staff was given by a speaker invited from another institution. It was a very attractive hospital that performed clinical work solidly while also having an academic atmosphere, and I rotated through three departments: hematology, neurology and gastroenterology. In my first rotation at CHOP, I belonged to the consult team in hematology. At CHOP, hematology and oncology are separate, and each has its own specialist professor. Fellows are to train in both departments, but I mainly saw hematology patients. One attending physician oversaw both inpatients and consults, with two fellows under him, and in the inpatient service several residents and students were in charge as well. The consult team consisted of only three people, the attending, the fellow and me as the student, so I was in the fortunate situation of having a senior physician all to myself as a student. Every morning from 8:15, the ward staff gathered for what was called rounds, where inpatients were presented and discussed. In the morning, when there was a new consult I went to see the patient, and when there was none I accompanied the attending on rounds of the inpatients. In the afternoon, I went around with the fellow to examine the consult patients we were following up, presented the patients in front of the attending, and then did rounds again. The hematology service at CHOP is known for its management of sickle cell disease, and many patients whose symptoms had worsened, for example triggered by infections, were hospitalised. Many of the consults were patients in whom an abnormality of the coagulation system had been found in screening blood tests, and in such cases we proposed a testing plan and followed them up. Sometimes consults came with complicated and urgent problems such as bleeding that would not stop, and we dealt with them by making full use of our specialist knowledge of transfusion and hemostasis.

In the first week after I started the clerkship, I struggled just to get used to the speed of the English, and I was often at a loss as to what was expected of a medical student. From around the third week, however, I became able to go through the whole sequence of conducting a medical interview and physical examination of the patient and the family, compiling the history and test results in the chart, and presenting to the senior physician. In particular, taking a detailed history was the students' job, and what I investigated, wrote in the chart and said in the presentation became the official record as it was, so I felt a heavy responsibility that I had never borne in clinical clerkships in Japan. In the next department, neurology, I also belonged to the consult team. Besides a fellow specialising in pediatric neurology, a resident aiming to become an adult neurologist at the neighbouring HUP came for several months to train in pediatric neurology, and I worked on consults with them. In pediatric neurology there were many consults for seizures, so detailed medical interviews were necessary, and I struggled again with medical conversation in English, which I had thought I had finally got used to. What impressed me in this department was the existence of the stroke team. I wondered what a stroke team could possibly be in a children's hospital, but it did not take long to notice that children with cerebrovascular disorders due to cerebrovascular abnormalities such as moyamoya disease or compression by tumours were hospitalised. The consult team first handled the initial examination and then contacted the team led by Dr. Ichord, and nurses and social workers together took care of the patient. I took my hat off to the dedication with which these women did their best while being considerate of the families who had been called to the ward or emergency room and were in a state of confusion. In neurology, I was given opportunities such as outpatient clerkships not only at CHOP but also at HUP, so I not only learned the difference between a children's hospital and an adult hospital but was also able to see the wide range of diseases that neurology covers. In the last department, gastroenterology, I was also assigned to consults. Often we were consulted because patients admitted to other departments showed poor weight gain. Unlike the departments I had trained in so far, in gastroenterology there were occasions requiring procedures such as endoscopy, and there were many times when I could only observe as a student, but after two months of clinical clerkship I had become used to medical interviews and presentations in English, so I think I was able to have a fulfilling clerkship. In gastroenterology there seemed to be many occasions when I was asked, "What kind of treatment is done in Japan?" For treatments of conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease, many pieces of evidence have been reported from Japan, and I could see that they are valued in clinical practice in the United States too. It was a scene in which I strongly felt that what is asked of doctors and students who have received a foreign medical education in the United States is not to imitate American medicine but an attitude of setting differences against each other and aiming for better medical care. Besides these clerkships within the hospital, meeting various people was also a great gain of studying abroad. Neuroscience research is thriving at Penn, and its number of National Institutes of Health (NIH) grants was once the highest in the country. I had the chance to visit the Center for Neurodegenerative Disease Research, which plays a part in this, and to talk with Professor Trojanowski, one of the center's directors.

The room I was shown into by Dr. 瓜生, a Japanese researcher, had lab benches lined up in several rows, and researchers of various backgrounds, with medical degrees (MD) and doctorates of science (PhD), were doing research together. The atmosphere, in which researchers from different fields repeatedly discussed with each other and tried to do research by bringing together one another's strengths, was very impressive. Finally, I would like to thank the many people, beginning with the Dean and the doctors of the International Exchange Office, thanks to whose consideration my study abroad was made possible. In particular, I thank Dr. 西崎彰 and Jason Liu, who looked after me in Philadelphia, and 早野聡, who trained with me at CHOP and shared joys and hardships with me both inside and outside the hospital.
